title: Bhai Gurdas, the man
hook: the scribe who, tradition says, was once tested and forgiven by Guru Hargobind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Ganga walked to Baba Buddha with bread she'd made herself. Your line was simple bread, big blessing. Did a plain meal reach someone? Today, a man the path has met before, seen up close. Day eight hundred ten.

A letter arrives at a king's court in Banaras, far from Punjab. It's from Guru Hargobind, and it says something strange. A thief of mine is hiding in your city. Find him, tie his hands, and send him back to me. The king's men go looking. And before they find anyone, a quiet, learned man steps forward and says: that's me. I'm the one he means. The thief is the Guru's own scribe. Today: Bhai Gurdas, the man.
screen: `A LETTER TO BANARAS.` → `FIND MY THIEF AND TIE HIS HANDS.` → `THAT'S ME.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas is a name this path has met as a writer. Tradition says he wrote out the Granth as Guru Arjan dictated it, and Sikhs speak of his own Vars as a key to the Guru's word. So it's a surprise that the story Sikhs tell about him as a man is a story of failure. Tradition tells it in more than one version. In a well-known one, Guru Hargobind sent him to Kabul with money to buy horses. He made the bargain, and went into his tent to fetch the payment. And the money wasn't there. Some tellings say it had turned to stones. Standing there, with the dealers waiting outside, he panicked. He was the Guru's trusted man, and he couldn't pay. So he slipped out the back of the tent and ran, all the way to Banaras, where nobody knew him. Some tellings add a reason for the test: that he had come to feel sure no true Sikh could ever waver. Then came the letter about the thief. He knew at once who was meant. He gave himself up, and was led back with his hands tied. And in front of Guru Hargobind, tradition says, he answered in verse: admitting he had failed, and asking for mercy the way a child asks a parent. The Guru forgave him, and he stayed in the Guru's house until the end of his life. Here's what's striking. Sikhs didn't hide this story to protect a great name. They kept it. The man tradition credits with writing out the Granth was tested, ran, came back, and was forgiven. The tradition seems to want everyone to know: even he was tested.
screen: `THE SCRIBE AND POET.` · `SENT TO KABUL, THE MONEY GONE.` · `HE RAN TO BANARAS.` · `BROUGHT BACK, AND FORGIVEN.` · then, large: `EVEN HE WAS TESTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive someone's lapse. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one person who let you down in a small way recently. A late reply, a dropped promise, a moment they ran instead of facing something. Don't replay it. Just see them, the way Guru Hargobind saw a frightened man with tied hands. Notice whether you've been keeping them in the thief's role. On each breath out, loosen the knot a little. You don't have to tell them anything yet. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Gurdas. The scribe and poet who, tradition says, failed a test, ran, came back with his hands tied, and was forgiven by Guru Hargobind. Today's word.
Your line: even he was tested. Today, when someone falls short, including you, remember the Guru's scribe ran too, and let one lapse be forgiven. Day eight hundred ten.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bhai Gurdas as the scribe of the Granth and the author of the Vars, which are sung in gurdwaras, and they tell the story of his test and forgiveness as part of who he was.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Bhai Gurdas; Bhai, brother, is a title of respect for a learned or devoted Sikh.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bhai Gurdas was simply the great scribe, beyond reproach.
what it means: tradition remembers him also as a man who failed a test, ran, and was forgiven.
what a scholar hears: the Kabul story survives in several versions, and tradition links his verse asking forgiveness to his return.

sources.ref: Bhai Gurdas's test and forgiveness, Sikh tradition

notes: The Kabul horses, the empty money bag (or stones), the flight to Banaras, the letter to the Raja of Banaras and the return with tied hands follow the common telling; versions differ. Confirm the version.
'Some tellings add a reason for the test: that he had come to feel sure no true Sikh could ever waver' is a paraphrase of a common explanation; confirm.
Tradition links a specific Var stanza (often said to be in Var 36) to his plea for forgiveness; the script only says 'he answered in verse'. A Keeper may want to name it.
'Sikhs call them a key to the Guru's word' (Guru Arjan's description of the Vars as the key, kunji, to gurbani): confirm wording.
'Stayed in the Guru's house until the end of his life': confirm.
Editor: 'the man who wrote the Granth out by hand' reframed as 'the man tradition credits with writing out the Granth' (claims rule).
